title: Out of Egypt: The Passover Story
bigQuestion: What does the Torah say happened when the people left Egypt, and why do Jewish families tell it every year?

story.title: The Youngest Child Asks
story.kicker: It is the first night of Passover, and the smallest person at the table has the biggest job.
paragraphs: It is spring in Chicago. Sam's family sits at a long table. There is flat bread on a plate. It is called matzah. There is a cup of wine. There is a plate with a green herb and a bitter herb. Sam is the youngest child at the table.
Sam's grandma nods at him. It is time. Sam stands up. He asks, "Why is this night different from all other nights?" Everyone smiles. This is the question the youngest child asks every year.

Sam's uncle opens a small book. It is called the Haggadah. That means "the telling." He says, "Tonight we tell a story from the Torah. Long ago, our people were slaves in Egypt. Then they walked out free."

Sam listens. He hears about a baby in a basket. He hears about a bush on fire. He hears about a king who said no. He hears about a sea that opened. Sam looks at the flat bread. "Why is it flat?" he asks. "Wait," says Grandma. "That is part of the story."
story.think: Why do you think the youngest child gets to ask the big question at the Passover table?

lessons.title: Slaves in Egypt
lessons.mainIdea: The Torah says Jacob's family grew into a people, and a Pharaoh made them slaves.
reading: The second book of the Torah is called Shemot. That means "Names." Its English name is *Exodus*. It starts with a list of names. They are the sons of Jacob who came to Egypt.
The Torah says the family grew and grew. It became a people. Then a new king ruled Egypt. A king of Egypt is called a *Pharaoh*. The story says this Pharaoh was afraid of the people.
So Pharaoh made them slaves. A slave has to work and cannot leave. The Torah says the people made bricks in the hot sun. Their lives were very hard.

words.d: the English name for Shemot, the second book of the Torah; it means going out
a king of Egypt in the Torah's story

look.title: Two Names for One Book
rows: Sons of Jacob named at the start
look.prompt: Which book of the Torah comes before Exodus? Say its name.

check.q: What does Shemot mean?
check.why: Shemot means "Names." The book starts with the names of Jacob's sons.

check.q: What is a Pharaoh?
check.why: In the Torah's story, the king of Egypt is called a Pharaoh.

check.q: What does the Torah say Pharaoh did to the people?
check.why: The Torah says Pharaoh made the people slaves. They had to make bricks.

lessons.title: A Baby in a Basket
lessons.mainIdea: The Torah says a mother hid baby Moses in a basket, and Pharaoh's daughter found him.
reading: The Torah says Pharaoh gave a cruel order about baby boys. One mother hid her baby. She made a *basket* and put him in it. She set it in the river reeds.
The baby's big sister watched from far away. Her name was *Miriam*. Then Pharaoh's daughter came to the river. She saw the basket. She opened it and the baby cried.
Pharaoh's daughter felt sorry for him. Miriam ran up. She said, "I know a woman who can feed him." It was the baby's own mother! Pharaoh's daughter named the baby *Moses*.

words.d: the small boat of reeds that held baby Moses in the Torah's story
Moses's big sister, who watched the basket and later sang by the sea
the baby in the basket, who grew up to lead the people out of Egypt

look.title: Look at the River
look.text: Look at the river. Tall reeds grow at the edge. A small basket floats between them. A girl hides behind the reeds and watches. Then a princess and her helpers walk down to the water. The princess points at the basket.
look.prompt: What do you think the girl behind the reeds is feeling? What is she waiting for?

check.q: Where did the mother put the baby's basket?
check.why: The Torah says she put the basket in the reeds at the edge of the river.

check.q: Who watched the basket from far away?
check.why: Miriam was the baby's big sister. She watched to see what would happen.

check.q: Who does the Torah say found the baby?
check.why: Pharaoh's daughter found the basket and named the baby Moses.

lessons.title: A Bush That Did Not Burn Up
lessons.mainIdea: The Torah says God spoke to Moses from a burning bush and sent him back to Egypt.
reading: Moses grew up. He left Egypt and became a shepherd. One day he saw a strange thing. A *bush* was on fire. But the fire did not burn it up.
The Torah says God spoke to Moses from the bush. God told Moses to go back to Egypt. God said to tell Pharaoh to let the people go.
Moses was scared. He said, "Who am I?" The Torah says God told him, "I will be with you." Moses's brother Aaron went with him to help him speak.

words.d: a small tree; in the Torah's story, God spoke to Moses from a bush on fire

look.title: The Bush on Fire
look.text: the bush burned with fire, and the bush was not consumed.
look.prompt: "Consumed" means burned up. What was strange about this fire?

check.q: What was strange about the bush?
choices: It burned but did not burn up
check.why: The Torah says the bush was on fire, but the fire did not burn it up.

check.q: What did God tell Moses to do, in the story?
check.why: The Torah says God sent Moses back to Egypt to tell Pharaoh to let the people go.

check.q: Who went with Moses to help him speak?
check.why: Aaron was Moses's brother. The Torah says he went along to help Moses speak.

lessons.title: Pharaoh Says No
lessons.mainIdea: The Torah says Moses told Pharaoh to let the people go, and ten plagues came when he said no.
reading: Moses and Aaron went to Pharaoh. They said, "Let my people go." Pharaoh said no. He made the people work even harder.

The Torah says ten *plagues* came to Egypt. A plague is a big trouble. The river turned red. Frogs hopped everywhere. Bugs came. Animals got sick. Hail fell. Locusts ate the plants. The sky went dark.
After each plague, Moses asked again. Pharaoh still said no. The last plague was the saddest of all. Then, the Torah says, Pharaoh finally said, "Go."

words.d: a big trouble; the Torah tells of ten plagues that came to Egypt

look.title: Four Small Words
look.text: Let My people go, that they may hold a feast unto Me in the wilderness.
look.prompt: Who is talking to Pharaoh here, and who is the message from?

check.q: What did Moses and Aaron say to Pharaoh?
check.why: The Torah says Moses and Aaron told Pharaoh, "Let my people go."

check.q: How many plagues does the Torah say came to Egypt?
check.why: The Torah tells of ten plagues. Frogs and darkness were two of them.

check.q: What is a plague?
check.why: A plague is a big trouble. The river turning red was one plague.

lessons.title: Bread With No Time to Rise
lessons.mainIdea: The Torah says the people left Egypt so fast their bread had no time to rise; Jewish families eat matzah to remember.
reading: The Torah says the people left Egypt at night. They had to hurry. Their bread dough had no time to rise. So it baked flat. Flat bread like this is called *matzah*.
That night is called *Passover*. In Hebrew it is Pesach. The Torah says the people put a mark on their doors. The last plague passed over their homes.
Every spring, Jewish families eat matzah for a week. They do this to remember. Flat bread means "we left in a hurry."

words.d: flat bread with no time to rise; Jewish families eat it at Passover
the spring holiday when Jewish families remember leaving Egypt

look.title: Two Kinds of Bread
look.text: Look at two plates. On one plate is a tall, soft loaf of bread. It took hours to rise. On the other plate is matzah. It is flat and crisp, with little holes. It baked in a few minutes.
look.prompt: Which bread would you take if you had to leave right now? Why does the Passover table have that one?

check.q: Why was the bread flat?
choices: It had no time to rise
It got wet in the sea
check.why: The Torah says the people left in a hurry. Their dough had no time to rise.

check.q: What is flat bread with no time to rise called?
check.why: Matzah is the flat bread. Challah is the braided bread for Shabbat.

check.q: When do Jewish families eat matzah for a week?
check.why: At Passover, Jewish families eat matzah to remember leaving Egypt.

lessons.title: The Sea Opens
lessons.mainIdea: The Torah says the sea opened, the people crossed, and Miriam led the singing.
reading: The people walked out of Egypt. They came to the edge of a *sea*. Then they looked back. Pharaoh had changed his mind. His army was coming.
The Torah says Moses held out his hand. A strong wind blew all night. The sea split in two. There was a dry path in the middle. The people walked across.
On the other side, they were safe. Moses and the people sang a song. Miriam took a drum. The women danced with her. They sang about the sea.

words.d: a very big body of water; the Torah says the sea opened so the people could cross

look.title: Miriam's Song
look.text: Sing ye to the LORD, for He is highly exalted: the horse and his rider hath He thrown into the sea.
look.prompt: Miriam sings this with a drum. What just happened that made her want to sing?

check.q: What does the Torah say happened at the sea?
choices: It split and made a dry path
check.why: The Torah says the sea split in two. The people walked on a dry path.

check.q: Who took a drum and led the women in dancing?
check.why: The Torah says Miriam took a drum, and the women danced and sang with her.

check.q: Why did the people look back and feel scared?
check.why: The Torah says Pharaoh changed his mind and sent his army after the people.

lessons.title: Telling It Every Year
lessons.mainIdea: Jewish families retell the Exodus story every year at a Passover meal called the Seder.
reading: Every spring, Jewish families sit down for a special meal. It is called the *Seder*. Seder means "order." The meal goes in a set order, step by step.
At the Seder, the youngest child asks four questions. The first is, "Why is this night different?" Then the family tells the story. A baby, a bush, a king, a sea.
There is matzah. There is a bitter herb for the hard years. There is a sweet mix for the bricks. Many Jewish families in Chicago hold a Seder every year.

words.d: the Passover meal where Jewish families tell the Exodus story in order
the small book that tells the story at the Seder; it means "the telling"

look.title: On the Seder Table
rows: Days of Passover in the Torah
look.cite: Exodus (Shemot) 12:15 for seven days; the four questions and four cups from the Passover Haggadah as Jewish tradition keeps it
look.prompt: How many questions does the youngest child ask? Try asking one.

check.q: What does Seder mean?
check.why: Seder means "order." The Passover meal goes step by step.

check.q: Who asks the questions at the Seder?
check.why: At the Seder, the youngest child asks the four questions.

check.q: What is the small book used at the Seder called?
check.why: The Haggadah is the book that tells the story. Its name means "the telling."

review.q: What is the English name for the book Shemot?
review.why: Shemot is the Hebrew name. Exodus is the English name for the same book.

review.q: Who does the Torah say watched the baby's basket?
review.why: Miriam, the baby's big sister, watched the basket in the reeds.

review.q: Where does the Torah say God spoke to Moses?
review.why: The Torah says God spoke to Moses from a bush that burned but did not burn up.

review.q: What did Pharaoh say when Moses asked him to let the people go?
review.why: The Torah says Pharaoh kept saying no. Ten plagues came before he said go.

review.q: Why do Jewish families eat matzah at Passover?
choices: To remember leaving Egypt in a hurry
review.why: Matzah is flat because the bread had no time to rise. It helps families remember.

review.q: What did Miriam do after the people crossed the sea?
choices: She sang and danced with a drum
review.why: The Torah says Miriam took a drum, and the women sang and danced with her.
